references.text: The priests who approach the Lord are mentioned in connection with consecration, indicating that young men served in a priestly role before the Levitical priesthood was established.
Jethro offered burnt offerings and peace offerings to God, similar types of sacrifices mentioned here as burnt offerings and fellowship offerings.
Detailed instructions for burnt offerings, which were performed by Israel's young men at this time.
The laws concerning the peace offering (shelamim) that was sacrificed during this covenant ceremony.
Noah built an altar and offered burnt offerings, an early example of burnt offerings before the Mosaic law.
Abraham offered a ram as a burnt offering in place of Isaac, an example of burnt offerings during the patriarchal period.
The book of Hebrews refers to this covenant ceremony and the blood used to dedicate the covenant.
Cattle blood and burnt offerings point forward to Christ's perfect sacrifice, since the blood of bulls could not take away sins.
Both verses describe large, collective sacrificial celebrations where burnt offerings and peace offerings were presented for the entire people as part of a holy act.
Both verses highlight the performance of the peace offering (bull and ram) as a central element in establishing or confirming God's reconciliation with His people.
Leviticus 17:5 explains the theological necessity of bringing peace offerings to the Lord's altar, which clarifies the action in Exodus 24.
